title: Work shares in creation (CCC 2427)
tomorrow: which matters more: a job done well, or the love behind it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, night prayer: Jesus's last words in Luke, from a psalm, said again at Compline. The line was into thy hands.

Work gets talked about like a sentence to be served: the grind, the Sunday-night dread, the countdown to Friday. So here's an odd detail in Genesis. Before the serpent, before the fruit, before anything goes wrong, the first man already has a job. In the Douay-Rheims: "the Lord God took man, and put him into the paradise of pleasure, to dress it, and to keep it." Work, in paradise.
screen: `THE GRIND, THE DREAD.` → `BEFORE ANYTHING GOES WRONG.` → `A JOB IN PARADISE.`

segments.voice: So where does the curse come in? Read on. After the fall, in Genesis 3, God says the ground will bring forth thorns and thistles, and: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." What changes isn't that there's work. It's that work gets hard: thorns, sweat, frustration. The job was there first, in the garden, and it was good. The Catechism picks this up in a single paragraph. It says human work comes straight from people made in God's image and called to carry on the work of creation, together and for one another. Saint John Paul the Second wrote that through work, a person shares in the activity of the Creator. That's today's line: co-creators. Not creating from nothing; in Catholic teaching only God does that. But taking what's been made and carrying it further: flour into bread, a field into a harvest, a blank page into a plan. The Catechism adds that the hard part of work can be joined to Jesus, whom Mark's Gospel calls "the carpenter, the son of Mary." Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: in the Bible's own order, the job comes before the problem.
screen: `THORNS AND SWEAT CAME LATER.` · `MADE IN GOD'S IMAGE, TO WORK.` · `FLOUR INTO BREAD.` · `THE CARPENTER, THE SON OF MARY.` · then, large: `CO-CREATORS.`

segments.voice: Pick up one thing near you that someone made: a mug, a chair, the shirt you're wearing. Turn it over slowly and notice the work in it, the hands that shaped it and the earth it came from. Then let one task waiting for you tomorrow sit beside it, as your piece of the same carrying-on.
Work shares in creation. The Catechism's teaching that human work carries on what God began.
Pocket this one: co-creators, flour into bread, carrying on what God began. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1, and the Church's social teaching, from the Catechism to papal letters on labor, speaks of work as sharing in God's creating.
